entities.label: Person
entities.summary: Lucius Calpurnius Piso Caesoninus was a Roman senator and consul in 106 BCE, son of Lucius Calpurnius Piso Caesoninus, who was consul in 148 BC. He played a significant role in the Roman Senate, particularly in the affairs of the Second Triumvirate, which aimed to avenge the death of Julius Caesar. Piso Caesoninus was also involved in the Roman conquest of Dacia, a region in modern-day Romania, under the command of Emperor Trajan. His legacy is tied to the Roman Empire's expansion and the rise of the Julio-Claudian dynasty. A notable event in his life was his involvement in the Roman Senate's attempt to reform the Roman calendar, which ultimately led to the creation of the Julian calendar. The Julian calendar, introduced by Julius Caesar in 45 BCE, was revised by Piso Caesoninus to introduce a leap year every four years, a reform that would have a lasting impact on Western calendars.
